findings.title: Federated recovery codes are never marked as used and can be replayed
findings.body: After credentialManager().isValid() succeeds, this code only checks RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() on the fetched credential. For a local credential, Keycloak's recovery-code provider consumes the code as part of validation and persists that state; for a federated credential, validation is delegated to the user storage's CredentialInputValidator, which merely validates the input (as the test provider does) and does not update the hashed code list or its used flags. Nothing here calls updateCredential/disableCredentialType to persist consumption. Consequently the same federated recovery code can be reused indefinitely, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean will keep asking for the first unused code instead of advancing to the next code.

findings.title: Exhausted federated recovery credentials are not removed
findings.body: When allCodesUsed() is true, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...). That operation removes credentials from Keycloak's local credential store only; it does not delete or disable a credential owned by a federated user storage. Because getCredential() now preferentially returns the federated credential, an exhausted federated credential can remain configured after this call while a CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is also added, leaving stale/used codes in the external storage and potentially causing repeated setup or inconsistent configuredFor state.

findings.title: Raw recovery codes are sent to user storage instead of the hashed credential data
findings.body: credentialModel already contains the recovery codes in Keycloak's hashed credential representation, but createRecoveryCodesCredential discards that data and sends JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes), i.e. the plaintext codes, as the UserCredentialModel challenge response. A federated provider that persists the challenge response verbatim (the added BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does exactly that) will store usable recovery codes in plaintext, unlike local storage which stores hashes. Compromise of the federated store would therefore disclose valid recovery codes; the helper should pass the hashed credential data or clearly require/implement hashing in the storage contract.

findings.title: Federated recovery credential loses user label and generation time
findings.body: The UserCredentialModel sent to user storage is constructed only from credentialModel.getType() and the generated-code JSON. It does not carry credentialModel's userLabel or createdDate/generation time, even though RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(generatedCodes, generatedAtTime, generatedUserLabel) was built with those values in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction. Federated providers therefore cannot persist the label/date chosen at setup; the test provider substitutes the current time and a null label, so account/console displays and credential metadata for federated recovery codes will be wrong or empty.

findings.title: Federated recovery-code test does not verify single-use or code advancement
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin logs in once with the code at index 0 and logs out. It does not attempt to reuse the same code, log in again with the next code, verify that the login page requests the next code number, or verify behavior when all codes are exhausted. Those are the main behavioral differences between local hashed recovery credentials and federated validation, so the current test would pass even though federated codes remain replayable and never advance.
